confounds: The classes are imbalanced: 618 diagnosed users versus 5,464 controls; pooled raw post totals are therefore misleading. Headline rates above are per-user post shares plus user prevalence.
Diagnosed timelines averaged about 630 posts versus 528 for controls, so any-user prevalence remains exposure-sensitive even after rate normalization.
Explicit mental-health and treatment vocabulary may encode self-report, medication access, therapy participation, community membership, or annotation leakage rather than depression causality.
Quotation, lyric, joke, news, advocacy, and third-person detection used lexical heuristics and will leave residual context errors.
Demographic, age, occupation, topic, platform, engagement, reply/mention, and collection-time differences can explain activity, punctuation, family, and positive-affect effects.

Feature redundancy is substantial: first-person post/token shares rho 0.791; mental-health/treatment rho 0.702; mental-health/anxiety rho 0.659. Do not treat correlated lexical families as independent evidence.

caveats: First-person language can occur in quotations, roleplay, replies, or ordinary autobiographical posting.
The two measurements are redundant; their Spearman correlation was 0.791.
findings.evidence_summary: The strongest generic signal was elevated first-person usage, surviving both post-share and token-share normalization.
findings.prompt_guidance: Use as a weak contextual feature, not as a diagnostic marker; combine with content and context filters.

quantitative_support.effect: Control-direction gap of 0.45 percentage points; AUC 0.469; control higher in all four folds.
Control-direction differences were stable: exclamation rate 5.13% vs 7.12%, ellipsis rate 6.20% vs 8.41%.

negative_results: Sleep-related vocabulary was not robust: mean post share was 2.56% diagnosed vs 2.51% control, with fold directions +,−,+,−.
Self-worth/denigration was near-null: 1.47% vs 1.39% mean post share, AUC 0.535, and one fold reversal.
Collective-pronoun and token-level negation contrasts were weak or unstable.
Self-harm-specific patterns were sparse; normalized-rate direction reversed in one fold despite higher user prevalence.
